readings.title: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
body: Let’s stop calling them “soft skills” — and call them “real skills” instead
We persist in hiring and training as if we’re running a bowling squad, as if easily measured skills are all that matter.

What causes successful organizations to fail ? What makes stocks fade, innovations slow, customers jump ship? We can agree that certain skills are essential. That hiring coders who can’t code, salespeople who can’t sell, or architects who can’t design is a waste. But these skills — let’s call them vocational skills — have become the backbone of the recruitment process.

But how do you explain that similar organizations, with similarly vocationally skilled people, find themselves with very different outcomes? Most of the textbooks that students experience and the tests they take are about vocational skills, the checkboxes that have to be checked to get a job. By misdefining “vocational” and focusing on these allegedly essential skills, we’ve diminished the value of the other skills that matter.

We give too little respect to the other skills when we call them “soft” and imply that they’re optional. What actually separates thriving organizations from struggling ones are the difficult-to-measure attitudes, processes and perceptions of the people who do the work.

Vocational skills can be taught: You’re not born knowing engineering or copywriting or even graphic design, therefore they must be something we can teach. But we let ourselves off the hook when it comes to decision-making, eager participation, dancing with fear, speaking with authority, working in teams , seeing the truth, speaking the truth, inspiring others, doing more than we’re asked, caring and being willing to change things. We underinvest in this training, fearful that these things are innate and can’t be taught. Perhaps they’re talents. And so we downplay them, calling them soft skills, making it easy for us to move on to something seemingly more urgent.

At scale, organizations pay less attention to soft skills when hiring because we’ve persuaded ourselves that vocational skills are impersonal and easier to measure. If it’s easier to test for, it seems more important when selecting our team.
And we fire slowly (and retrain rarely) when these skills are missing, because we’re worried about stepping on toes, being called out for getting personal or possibly wasting time on a lost cause.

But these skills can all be learned, as obvious skills like chess or typing can be learned. We learn them accidentally, by osmosis, by the collisions we have with teachers, parents, bosses and the world. Even though they’re more difficult to measure, that doesn’t mean we can’t improve them, can’t practice them or can’t change the way we do our work.

Let’s stop calling them soft. They’re interpersonal skills. Leadership skills. The skills of charisma and diligence and contribution. But these modifiers, while accurate, somehow edge them away from the vocational skills, the skills that we actually hire for, the skills we measure a graduate degree on.
So let’s uncomfortably call them real skills instead.
Real because they work, because they’re at the heart of what we need today.
Real because even if you’ve got the vocational skills, you’re no help to us without these human skills, the things that we can’t write down or program a computer to do.
Real skills can’t replace vocational skills, of course. What they can do is amplify the things you’ve already been measuring.
Imagine a team member with all the traditional vocational skills: productive, skilled, experienced. A resume that can prove it. That’s a fine baseline.

Now add to it. Perceptive, charismatic, driven, focused, goal-setting, inspiring and motivated. Generous, empathic and consistent. A deep listener , with patience. What happens to your organization when someone like that joins your team?
Writing in the Harvard Business Review , Lou Solomon reports that 69 percent of managers are uncomfortable communicating with their employees. I’d guess that many of the other 31 percent are lying.

Communicating with employees is uncomfortable because we’ve built systems of compliance and dominance that make it difficult. We ask people to leave their humanity at the door, then use authority to change behavior. We overlay corporate greed and short-term thinking with a human desire to create work that matters.

How do we build people-centric organizations while also accepting the fact that two thirds of our managers (presumably well paid, well trained and integral to our success) are so uncomfortable doing an essential part of their job that they admitted it to a stranger?

In a recent survey, the Graduate Management Admission Council reported that although MBAs were strong in analytical aptitude, quantitative expertise and information-gathering ability, they were sorely lacking in other critical areas that employers find equally attractive: strategic thinking, written and oral communication, leadership and adaptability . Are these mutually exclusive? Must we trade one for the other?

The foundation of all real skills is this one: the confidence and permission to talk to one another. Not to manage, belittle, intimidate or control. Simply to seek to be understood and to do the work to understand.

readings.cn:
##段落
让我们别再称它们为“软技能”——而应改称“真技能”
2023年6月9日
/
赛斯·戈丁
Facebook
X
LinkedIn
Reddit
WhatsApp
黛博拉·斯皮尔曼
我们一直以经营保龄球队的方式来进行招聘和培训，仿佛只有易于衡量的技能才至关重要。

##段落
是什么导致成功组织走向失败？是什么让股票黯然失色、创新放缓、客户纷纷流失？我们可以达成共识：某些技能不可或缺。招聘不会写代码的程序员、不会销售的销售员，或不会设计的建筑师，纯属浪费。但这些技能——我们姑且称之为职业技能——已成为招聘流程的核心支柱。

##段落
但如何解释那些拥有类似职业技能人才、结构相似的机构，最终却走向截然不同的结局？学生所接触的大多数教科书和考试，都围绕职业技能展开，即那些为获得工作而必须勾选的硬性指标。由于对“职业”的误读，并过度聚焦于这些所谓的关键技能，我们贬低了其他同样重要的技能的价值。

##段落
当我们把这些其他技能称为“软”技能，并暗示它们可有可无时，我们便给予它们太少的尊重。真正将蓬勃发展的组织与苦苦挣扎的组织区分开来的，是那些难以量化的态度、流程与认知——来自那些真正执行工作的人。

##段落
职业技能是可以教授的：你并非天生就懂工程、文案写作，甚至平面设计，因此它们必然是可教之物。但在决策、积极参与、与恐惧共舞、有权威地表达、团队协作、洞察真相、直言不讳、激励他人、超越本职、用心关怀以及勇于推动变革等方面，我们却让自己轻易脱身。我们对这些培训投入不足，担心这些品质是与生俱来的，无法后天习得。或许它们是天赋。于是我们轻描淡写，称其为“软技能”，以便轻松转向某些看似更紧迫的事项。

##段落
在规模化组织中，招聘时对软技能的关注度较低，因为我们说服自己相信：职业技能是非个人化的，且更容易衡量。如果某项技能更容易测试，在选拔团队时它就显得更为重要。

##段落
而当这些软技能缺失时，我们却迟迟不采取行动（也很少进行再培训），因为我们担心踩到别人的脚，担心被指责过于针对个人，或担心在一个没有希望的事情上浪费时间。

##段落
但这些技能都是可以习得的，就像下棋或打字这类显而易见的技能一样。我们是通过耳濡目染、潜移默化，通过与老师、父母、老板以及这个世界的碰撞而偶然习得的。尽管它们更难衡量，但这并不意味着我们无法提升它们，无法加以练习。

我们无法改变工作方式吗？  
当然可以。  
别再称它们为“软技能”了。它们是人际交往技能，是领导力技能，是魅力、勤奋和贡献的技能。但这些修饰词，虽然准确，却不知何故将它们从职业技能、我们真正招聘时看重的技能、我们衡量研究生学位的技能中边缘化了。  
所以，让我们不舒服地称它们为“真正的技能”吧。  
之所以说“真正”，是因为它们有效，因为它们是我们今天所需的核心。  
之所以说“真正”，是因为即使你拥有职业技能，但没有这些人际技能——那些我们无法写下来或编程让计算机去做的事情——你对我们也毫无帮助。  
真正的技能当然不能取代职业技能。它们能做的是放大你已经在衡量的那些东西。  
想象一个拥有所有传统职业技能的团队成员：高效、熟练、经验丰富。一份能证明这些的简历。那是一个不错的基线。  
现在再加上这些：敏锐、有魅力、有驱动力、专注、目标明确、激励人心且积极主动。慷慨、富有同理心且始终如一。耐心倾听，深度理解。当这样的人加入你的团队时，你的组织会发生什么变化？  
在《哈佛商业评论》上，卢·所罗门报道称，69%的管理者不善于与员工沟通。我猜另外31%中的许多人在撒谎。  
与员工沟通之所以不自在，是因为我们建立了合规和支配的系统，使沟通变得困难。我们要求人们把人性留在门外，然后用权威来改变行为。我们将企业贪婪和短期思维与人类创造有意义工作的渴望叠加在一起。  
我们如何建立以人为中心的组织，同时接受这样一个事实：我们三分之二的管理者（想必薪水丰厚、训练有素、对我们的成功至关重要）在做一个基本工作部分时如此不自在，以至于向陌生人坦白了这一点？  
在最近一项调查中，研究生管理入学委员会报告称，尽管MBA在分析能力、定量专长和信息收集能力方面很强，但他们在雇主同样看重的其他关键领域严重欠缺：战略思维、书面和口头沟通、领导力和适应性。这些是相互排斥的吗？我们必须牺牲一个来换取另一个吗？  
所有真正技能的基础是这一点：拥有自信和许可去相互交谈。不是去管理、贬低、恐吓或控制。仅仅是寻求被理解，并努力去理解。  
摘自赛斯·戈丁的《意义的歌：团队新宣言》，经企鹅兰登书屋旗下Portfolio出版社同意转载。

readings.title: You want a baby. Is it ethical to choose surrogacy?
body: The Highlight You want a baby. Is it ethical to choose surrogacy? ﻿The line between medically necessary and elective surrogacy isn’t as tidy as people assume. by Sigal Samuel Updated Aug 23, 2026, 12:33 PM UTC Gift Pete Gamlen for Vox Sigal Samuel is a correspondent for Vox’s Future Perfect. She writes primarily about the future of consciousness, tracking advances in artificial intelligence and neuroscience and their staggering ethical implications. Before joining Vox, Sigal was the religion editor at the Atlantic. Editor’s note, August 23, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published in February. This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here . I’m a woman in my 30s and I think I want to have a child, but I have a health condition that makes it harder (not impossible) to get pregnant than for most women. It would also make pregnancy more uncomfortable and physically disfiguring than it is for many pregnant people. It wouldn’t be permanently disabling, but the physical effects would be bad enough that I really don’t want to be pregnant. I’m fortunate enough that I can probably afford to get a surrogate through a reputable agency. But surrogacy is frowned upon and often considered unethical. Long ago, I knew someone who said she loved the idea of being pregnant and providing gestation as a service to other people, so maybe in theory, it is possible for someone to freely choose to be a surrogate without being coerced by financial need? But even if it could be done ethically, there’s such a stigma around it and I fear being judged by friends and family. There seems to be a sense that there’s something wrong, unnatural, selfish, or unwomanly in wanting to have a biological child but not wanting your own body to be the vessel for it. Plus, it’s not like I’m the only person in the world for whom pregnancy would suck. I think my experience probably would be worse than average, but pregnancy is just an unpleasant thing overall so I don’t think I can claim it would be so uniquely bad for me that I’m justified in wanting to pay to use someone else’s body. I’d love your help with this. Dear Really Don’t Want To Be Pregnant, There are some ethical questions about surrogacy that it’s genuinely worth asking, and some that I don’t want you to devote another second to — so let’s start there. As you said, there’s a cultural stigma around not wanting to turn your body into a vessel for childbearing — it’s deemed “wrong” or “unwomanly.” But that idea is pure garbage. The idea that there’s some “proper” way to be a woman is a patriarchal construct; anyone who tells you you’re “unwomanly” for not wanting to gestate is reflecting sexist expectations that women’s bodies should be available for reproductive labor. So to the extent that your fear of being judged is about that, please don’t give it another thought. But of course, there are real moral questions that surrogacy brings up. I’ll tell you right off the bat that I do think surrogacy can be ethically justifiable in some situations. First, it helps that surrogacy is not one monolithic thing. There’s a big distinction between commercial surrogacy (where you pay someone to carry a baby) and altruistic surrogacy (the unpaid version, where the surrogate carries the baby as a literal labor of love). It’s not easy to find an altruistic surrogate — after all, pregnancy is dangerous business — but I agree with your intuition that if you’re lucky enough to know someone willing to volunteer for the role, opting for that is a good way to avoid most concerns about commodification or exploitation. Unethical surrogacy industries are booming in places like Georgia, Ukraine, and Cyprus. But there’s a moral difference between hiring a surrogate there versus in the US. When someone can get pregnant but doesn’t want to for psychological reasons, their case is often deemed “elective.” But a mental health need can also be a medical need. “Epistemic injustice” refers to a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. People who say they know they have a mental health need that makes pregnancy too risky often aren’t taken seriously, but that’s starting to change. Within commercial surrogacy, a second distinction has to do with where the surrogate lives. There’s a moral difference between hiring a surrogate in a developing country and hiring one in, say, the US. In countries like Georgia , for example, surrogacy agencies have been known to recruit at domestic violence shelters — some women see surrogacy as the only way to win financial freedom from an abusive spouse. Ukraine , Cyprus , and several others are also known to have ethically problematic surrogacy industries. But American surrogates are typically not low-income; they’re usually middle-class white women with husbands and kids of their own, and they have other economic opportunities available to them. The better surrogacy agencies screen out poor women, who are at risk of coercion. That empirical context means there’s less (though not zero) potential for exploitation in the US, compared with international surrogacy. Another reason I think surrogacy can be ethically justifiable is that for many, many people, the urge to have kids — including ones who are biologically related to them — feels like a need and not just a want. Many opponents of surrogacy argue that nobody has a “right” to a biological child, so if you can’t or don’t want to be pregnant, too bad. And those opponents are right that nobody has an absolute right to have a baby — otherwise, the state would be obligated to ensure surrogates, egg donors, and sperm donors were made available regardless of their own willingness to participate! But people may still have a qualified right — the kind of right that we generally honor but that can be restricted to protect the interests of others. When it comes to people who are physically unable to create a biological child — when they have what doctors call a “medical indication” — I think the qualified right to have a kid means that surrogacy can be ethical, provided it meets certain criteria like informed consent. But your situation is trickier because it’s not impossible for you to get pregnant — it’s more that, for certain reasons, you don’t want to. Typically, your case would be referred to as “elective surrogacy.” Some professionals will refuse to arrange surrogacy if they deem it elective rather than medically indicated. And yet, doctors are increasingly recognizing that the line between “medically indicated” and “elective” is not so tidy. While elective surrogacy is often associated with vanity — it brings to mind a celebrity who doesn’t want to be pregnant because she doesn’t want to “mess up” her figure — it’s not like everyone in the elective camp is there for cosmetic reasons. What about someone who could get pregnant but is deathly afraid of giving birth because she had a traumatic experience — like, say, her best friend dying in childbirth? Or what about someone who’s trans and who physically could carry a pregnancy, but who knows it would cause such gender dysphoria that there’s a risk of serious psychological harm? Shouldn’t a mental health need be considered a type of medical need? These are not hypothetical experiences — real people have testified to them — but they often haven’t been taken seriously as medical needs. I suspect that these people have endured what the contemporary philosopher Miranda Fricker calls “epistemic injustice.” Epistemic injustice refers to “a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower.” When society denies someone the credibility to assess their own life experience, or discounts an important part of that experience because of a gap in our collective interpretive resources, that can be an example of epistemic injustice. I think people who fall in between medical categories are too often at risk of being wronged in this way, and I don’t want to see that happen to you. So I want to acknowledge that I don’t know what health condition you’re referring to when you say you have a condition that would “make pregnancy more uncomfortable and physically disfiguring than it is for many pregnant people.” Since I don’t know the details, I’d encourage you to ask yourself: How much more uncomfortable? How much more disfiguring? And how heavy and lasting a toll would that discomfort or disfigurement take on your overall well-being? Only you can really try to answer that last question, because the same effects can land differently for different people, depending on how well-resourced we are financially, socially, psychologically, and even spiritually. Once you’ve thought about how big and enduring the risk of harm is to you, try asking yourself this: Is the risk to you so much greater than the risk to a woman of average health that you feel comfortable transferring the risk of pregnancy and childbirth onto her? Some people will tell you that question is irrelevant. They will say that the only value that matters here is autonomy — yours and the potential surrogate’s — and if you and she both consent to a surrogacy contract, and she is not coerced into it by financial desperation, then that’s that! But there may be another important value at stake here: justice. Just fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does, and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here. As far as I can tell, your case is in a gray area — surrogacy is neither obviously “medically indicated” nor obviously “elective” based on the information you shared. If you ask yourself, “Do I think there’s a significant risk that carrying a child would significantly harm me?” and you answer “Yes!” — then some doctors would say surrogacy is medically indicated. But if the answer you feel bubbling up is, “Well…no, not really,” then you may be closer to the “elective” side of the spectrum. And then I think it becomes reasonable to inquire whether it feels fair to ask another woman to take on the considerable risks of pregnancy and childbirth. You wrote of pregnancy, “I don’t think I can claim it would be so uniquely bad for me that I’m justified in wanting to pay to use someone else’s body.” That suggests that you currently see yourself as more in the elective camp. I urge you to give yourself the space to really interrogate that with an equal measure of honesty and self-compassion. If honesty compels you to say you don’t feel justified in putting someone else’s body in harm’s way in a situation where she otherwise wouldn’t be, then maybe you’ve got your answer. But if you’re discounting the risk of psychological harm to yourself because you don’t think that “counts” as real need, please know that mental health is just as medically legitimate as physical health. And if you talk to a medical professional about the option of surrogacy, please talk to more than one so you’re less at risk of getting boxed into a category that doesn’t capture you right. At the end of the day, perhaps none of us can be a perfect interpreter even of ourselves. But you get to be the interpreter-in-chief — with both the power and responsibility that implies. This horrifying New York Times Magazine story about the global fertility industry captures why I do think it’s unethical to work with a surrogacy agency in a country like Georgia. These surrogates are not in a position to give informed consent. “ Is Cognitive Dissonance Actually a Thing? ” asked Shayla Love in the New Yorker recently. I now feel cognitive dissonance about all the times I thought I was feeling cognitive dissonance! Don’t miss “ I’m Kenyan. I Don’t Write Like ChatGPT. ChatGPT Writes Like Me .” This essay by Marcus Olang’, explaining why his writing is often mistaken for AI slop, is both surprising and maddening. Turns out it’s really hard to not write in the Queen’s English when an entire colonial legacy has drilled that style into you from birth. ##段落你想要一个宝宝。选择代孕是否合乎伦理？医疗必要性与选择性代孕之间的界限并不像人们想象的那样清晰。作者：西格尔·塞缪尔 更新于2026年8月23日，下午12:33 UTC 礼品 皮特·甘伦为Vox供稿 西格尔·塞缪尔是Vox“未来完美”栏目的记者。她主要撰写关于意识未来的文章，追踪人工智能和神经科学的进展及其惊人的伦理影响。加入Vox之前，西格尔曾是《大西洋月刊》的宗教编辑。编辑注，8月23日，上午8点（东部时间）：在西格尔·塞缪尔休产假期间，我们为您带来一些最受欢迎的“里程因人而异”专栏。以下这篇最初发布于2月。这个非传统建议专栏为您提供一个独特的框架，用来思考道德困境。它基于价值多元主义：即我们每个人都拥有多种同样有效但常常相互冲突的价值观。在此提交您的问题。我是一位三十多岁的女性，我觉得自己可能想要一个孩子，但我有一种健康状况，使得怀孕比大多数女性更难（并非不可能）。它也会让怀孕比许多孕妇更不舒服，身体上更变形。这不会造成永久性残疾，但身体影响会严重到我真的不想怀孕。我很幸运，可能负担得起通过信誉良好的机构找代孕妈妈。但代孕备受争议，常被认为不道德。很久以前，我认识一个人，她说她喜欢怀孕的想法，并愿意为他人提供妊娠服务，所以也许理论上，有人可以自由选择成为代孕者而不受经济需求的胁迫？但即使可以合乎伦理地做到，围绕它仍有很大污名，我害怕被朋友和家人评判。似乎有一种感觉，想要一个亲生孩子但不想让自己的身体成为载体，是错误、不自然、自私或不够女性化的。而且，我并不是世界上唯一一个怀孕会很糟糕的人。我想我的经历可能比平均水平更差，但怀孕总体上是件不愉快的事，所以我不认为我能声称它对我如此独特地糟糕，以至于我有理由花钱使用他人的身体。我希望你能帮我解决这个问题。亲爱的“真的不想怀孕”：关于代孕，有一些伦理问题确实值得追问，也有一些我不想让你再多花一秒钟去纠结——所以我们从后者开始吧。如你所说，有一种文化污名围绕着不想让自己的身体成为生育载体——这被视为“错误”或“不够女性化”。

但这个想法完全是胡说八道。认为存在某种“正确”的女性方式，是父权制的建构；任何告诉你，因为不想孕育就说你“不够女人”的人，反映的是性别歧视的期望，即女性的身体应可供生殖劳动使用。所以，如果你害怕被评判与此有关，请别再多想。当然，代孕确实引发了一些真实的道德问题。我直截了当地告诉你，我确实认为在某些情况下代孕在伦理上是可以辩护的。首先，代孕并非单一概念，这有助于理解。商业代孕（你付钱让别人怀孕）和利他代孕（无偿版本，代孕者作为纯粹的爱的劳动来怀孕）之间有重大区别。找到利他代孕者并不容易——毕竟，怀孕是危险的事——但我同意你的直觉，如果你幸运地认识愿意自愿承担这一角色的人，选择这种方式是避免大多数商品化或剥削担忧的好方法。不道德的代孕产业在格鲁吉亚、乌克兰和塞浦路斯等地蓬勃发展。但在那里雇佣代孕者与美国相比，存在道德差异。当有人能怀孕但因心理原因不想时，他们的案例常被视为“选择性”的。但心理健康需求也可以是医疗需求。“认知不公正”指的是对某人作为认知者身份的伤害。那些声称自己知道有心理健康需求使怀孕风险过高的人，往往不被认真对待，但这种情况正在改变。在商业代孕中，第二个区别与代孕者的居住地有关。在发展中国家雇佣代孕者与在美国等地方雇佣，存在道德差异。例如，在格鲁吉亚等国家，已知代孕机构会在家庭暴力庇护所招募——一些女性将代孕视为从虐待配偶那里赢得经济自由的唯一途径。乌克兰、塞浦路斯和其他几个国家也以存在伦理问题的代孕产业而闻名。但美国代孕者通常不是低收入者；她们通常是中产阶级白人女性，有自己的丈夫和孩子，并且有其他经济机会可用。较好的代孕机构会筛除贫困女性，因为她们面临胁迫风险。这种经验背景意味着，与国际代孕相比，美国代孕的剥削可能性较小（尽管不是零）。我认为代孕在伦理上可以辩护的另一个原因是，对许多人来说，生育孩子的强烈愿望——包括那些有血缘关系的——是真实且深刻的。

对他们而言——这感觉像是一种需要，而不仅仅是想要。许多反对代孕的人争辩说，没有人“有权”拥有一个亲生孩子，所以如果你不能或不想怀孕，那就没办法了。这些反对者说得对，没有人拥有绝对的生育权——否则，国家就有义务确保代孕者、卵子捐献者和精子捐献者无论自身意愿如何都能被提供！但人们可能仍然拥有一种有限的权利——这种权利我们通常尊重，但为了保护他人利益可以受到限制。对于身体上无法生育亲生孩子的人——当他们有医生所谓的“医学指征”时——我认为这种有限的生育权意味着代孕可以是合乎伦理的，前提是满足知情同意等某些标准。但你的情况更棘手，因为你并非不可能怀孕——而更多是出于某些原因，你不想要。通常，你的案例会被称为“选择性代孕”。一些专业人士如果认为代孕是选择性的而非医学指征，会拒绝安排。然而，医生们越来越认识到“医学指征”和“选择性”之间的界限并不那么清晰。虽然选择性代孕常与虚荣联系在一起——这让人想到某个不想怀孕以保持身材的名人——但并非所有选择阵营中的人都是出于美容原因。那些能怀孕却因创伤经历（比如闺蜜死于分娩）而极度恐惧生育的人呢？或者那些跨性别者，身体上能怀孕，但知道这会引发严重的性别焦虑，有心理伤害风险的人呢？心理健康需求难道不应该被视为一种医疗需求吗？这些并非假设性经历——真实的人们已经作证过——但它们往往没有被认真视为医疗需求。我怀疑这些人经历了当代哲学家米兰达·弗里克所称的“认知不公正”。认知不公正指的是“对某人在其作为认知者身份上的错误对待”。当社会否认某人评估自身生活经历的可信度，或因我们集体解释资源中的空白而忽视该经历的重要部分时，这可能是认知不公正的一个例子。我认为那些介于医学类别之间的人常常面临被如此错误对待的风险，而我不希望看到你遭遇这种情况。所以我想承认，我不知道你指的是什么健康状况，当你

你说你有一种情况，会让“怀孕比许多孕妇所经历的更加不适和身体毁损”。由于我不知道具体情况，我鼓励你问自己：有多不适？有多毁损？这种不适或毁损对你的整体幸福感会造成多严重、多持久的负担？只有你才能真正尝试回答最后一个问题，因为同样的影响对不同人可能产生不同的感受，取决于我们在经济、社交、心理甚至精神上的资源有多丰富。一旦你想清楚了风险对你有多大且多持久，试着问自己：你面临的风险是否比一个普通健康女性的风险大得多，以至于你愿意把怀孕和分娩的风险转移给她？有些人会告诉你这个问题无关紧要。他们会说，这里唯一重要的价值是自主权——你和潜在代孕者的自主权——如果你和她都同意代孕合同，且她不是因经济绝望而被胁迫，那就这样了！但这里可能还有另一个重要的价值：公平。只需填写这份匿名表格！新闻通讯订阅者会比其他人都先看到我的专栏，他们的问题将在未来版本中优先处理。在此注册。据我所知，你的情况处于灰色地带——基于你分享的信息，代孕既不是明显的“医学必要”，也不是明显的“选择性”。如果你问自己：“我认为怀孕是否会显著伤害我的风险很大吗？”并回答“是！”——那么一些医生会说代孕是医学必要的。但如果你感觉涌上来的答案是，“嗯……不，不太会，”那么你可能更接近“选择性”的一端。然后我认为，询问让另一个女性承担怀孕和分娩的巨大风险是否公平就变得合理了。你写道，对于怀孕，“我不认为我能声称它对我如此特别糟糕，以至于我有理由花钱使用别人的身体。”这表明你目前更倾向于将自己归入选择性阵营。我敦促你给自己空间，以同等程度的诚实和自我同情真正审视这一点。如果诚实迫使你说，在对方本不会处于危险的情况下，你觉得自己没有理由让别人身体冒险，那么也许你已经有了答案。但如果你因为认为心理健康不“算”真正的需求而低估了对自己心理伤害的风险，请知道心理健康在医学上与身体健康同样合法。如果你与医疗专业人士交谈，

如果您正在考虑代孕这一选项，请务必咨询多位专业人士，以免被局限在不适合您的分类中。归根结底，也许没有人能完美诠释我们自己，但您可以成为自己的首席诠释者——这既意味着权力，也意味着责任。

《纽约时报杂志》那篇关于全球生育产业的骇人报道，解释了为什么我认为在格鲁吉亚这样的国家与代孕机构合作是不道德的。那些代孕者并没有处于能够给予知情同意的地位。

“认知失调真的存在吗？”莎拉·洛夫最近在《纽约客》中问道。我现在对自己曾经以为感受到认知失调的每一次经历，都感到认知失调了！

千万别错过“我是肯尼亚人。我不像ChatGPT那样写作。ChatGPT像我一样写作。”这篇由马库斯·奥朗撰写的文章，解释了他为何常被误认为是在写AI垃圾内容，既令人惊讶又令人恼火。事实证明，当整个殖民遗产从出生起就将那种风格灌输给你时，很难不用女王英语写作。

readings.title: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do
body: Feeling unseen by your boss? Here’s what you can do

Ever have your hard work — including your successes — go unnoticed by your manager? Fixable , TED’s new podcast, is here to do just that — to fix the problems of everyday people who call in with their work woes.

In episode four , cohosts and top leadership coaches Frances Frei and Anne Morriss got to know Nai’a, a caller who struggled with receiving recognition after a major reorganization paired her with a new and preoccupied boss. Nai’a was going above and beyond to do her job well, but the lack of acknowledgement and encouragement — and even awareness — of her work was causing her to lose motivation.
Frances’s and Anne’s first piece of advice to Nai’a was simple: See the humanness of what’s going on — and of your manager.

“Sometimes the barrier to showing up as a great collaborator with your manager can be that there’s still some residual frustration about the situation,” Anne explained. “But that emotion is not going to be useful to you.”
Instead, they encouraged Nai’a to recognize the humanity of her manager and forgive them for making mistakes.
Frances and Anne also shared this strategy with her to practice: Choose curiosity over judgment.

Here’s how Frances put it: “You have a choice between judgment and curiosity, because both can’t exist at the same time. So if you have judgment about your manager, you can’t really be curious about their situation. And when you’re thinking of your manager as a person who’s got a lot of part-time jobs, how do we set them up for success?”

“The simplest expression of curiosity — which is truly a magical elixir in a workplace — is in the form of questions,” said Anne. For example, you could start by asking your manager what process works best for them to learn about your accomplishments and contributions. Or, you could focus on how you can make your meetings with them more productive by asking them, “How can our one-on-one time be of service to what we’re trying to achieve together?”

Another option: Be open about your concerns, and ask your manager what their vision of your success looks like. You could say something like, “Here’s my fear: I’m working really hard, and in this state of flux, I’m afraid that six months will go by and people are going to wonder whether or not I did a good job. So it’s just helpful for me to be clear — what is a good job and how can I help in getting that data for you?”

Across industries and across the world, many people are going through workplace reorganizations and other sweeping changes. And like Nai’a, it’s normal to feel anxious and stressed by what’s happening and to need to go through a readjustment period. Leading with questions — and seeing your boss as another human you’re collaborating with — can help you gain back some agency and autonomy.

“Try doing what you can, and marvel at how the other person changes as a result, as opposed to coming up with the list of how you would like the other person to change,” said Frances. “I think you’re going to be pleasantly surprised; that’s the beautiful part of this.”

No matter your job or business, you’ll find actionable advice on Fixable that can improve your workdays. In other episodes, learn how to overcome communication roadblocks, scale up your side project and lead more productive meetings. Plus: Click here for a chance to get your own work question answered on the show! Listen to Fixable now wherever you get your podcasts.
About the author Hayley Caldwell is a copywriter on the Audience Development team at TED.

##段落
你有没有过这样的经历：你的辛勤工作——包括你的成功——被经理视而不见？TED的新播客《Fixable》正是为此而来——帮助那些带着职场烦恼来电的普通人解决问题。

##段落
在第四集中，联合主持人兼顶级领导力教练弗朗西丝·弗雷和安妮·莫里斯认识了来电者奈阿，她在一次重大重组后被安排了一位新老板，而这位老板心不在焉，她因此苦于得不到认可。奈阿尽心尽力想把工作做好，但缺乏认可、鼓励——甚至关注——让她逐渐失去动力。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮给奈阿的第一条建议很简单：看清事情中的人性——以及你经理的人性。

##段落
“有时，阻碍你与经理成为优秀合作伙伴的，可能是对现状残留的挫败感，”安妮解释道，“但那种情绪对你没有任何帮助。”

##段落
相反，她们鼓励奈阿去认识经理的人性，并原谅他们犯错。

##段落
弗朗西丝和安妮还分享了这样一个策略让她练习：选择好奇，而非评判。

##段落
弗朗西丝是这样说的：“你在评判和好奇之间做选择，因为两者无法同时存在。所以如果你对经理有评判，你就无法真正对他们处境感到好奇。而当你把经理看作一个身兼数职的人时，我们该如何为他们创造成功条件？”

##段落
“好奇最简单的表达形式——它在职场中堪称灵丹妙药——就是提问，”安妮说。例如，你可以先问问经理，用什么方式让他们了解你的成就和贡献最有效。或者，你可以通过问“我们的一对一时间如何为我们共同目标服务？”来让与他们的会议更有成效。

##段落
另一个选择：坦率表达你的担忧，并询问经理他们对你成功的愿景是什么。你可以这样说：“我的担忧是：我工作非常努力，在这种变动时期，我担心六个月过去后，人们会怀疑我是否干得出色。所以对我来说，明确标准很有帮助——什么算干得好，我怎样才能帮你获取这些信息？”

##段落
放眼全球、横跨各行各业，许多人都在经历工作重组和其他大规模变革。和奈阿一样，面对正在发生的事情感到焦虑和压力，需要经历一段重新调整期，这都是正常的。

带着问题去沟通——把老板看作与你协作的另一个普通人——可以帮助你重新获得一些主动权和自主性。

“试着做你能做的，然后惊奇地观察对方因此发生的变化，而不是列出一堆你希望对方如何改变的要求，”弗朗西斯说。“我想你会惊喜的；这正是这件事的美妙之处。”

无论你从事什么工作或经营什么业务，你都能在《Fixable》中找到改善工作日的实用建议。在其他集数中，学习如何克服沟通障碍、扩展你的副业项目，以及主持更高效的会议。另外：点击这里，有机会让你自己的工作问题在节目中获答！现在就在你收听播客的任何平台收听《Fixable》。

body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff No new Canada tariffs — for now I regret to inform you that we still have to think about tariffs. by Cameron Peters Aug 19, 2026, 10:15 PM UTC Gift President Donald Trump speaks with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney at the G7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 16, 2026. Evelyn Hockstein/AFP via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump’s planned Canada tariffs are off — for now. What happened? Trump had previously threatened 50-percent tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, but delayed them late on Tuesday, hours before they were set to take effect. In a social media post, he wrote that the tariffs were on hold for “a three day period, based on the fact that Canada and the U.S.A., subject to the finalization of documents, have a DEAL!” Is there actually a deal? We’ll find out in the next three days. Trump’s claims should always be taken with a grain of salt, and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said only that “substantial progress” had been made toward a deal, with “important work still to be done.” On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US could reduce previous tariffs on Canadian goods —which applied to cars, steel, and aluminum — as part of a potential trade deal. Trump has also suggested that a deal could resurrect the Keystone XL oil pipeline. Can Trump still impose new tariffs? He can. Earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s use of a specific law, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, to impose tariffs. In doing so, the Court ended many of his most sweeping tariffs and took away his favorite way to impose them. He has plenty of other tools to keep at it, though, albeit on a more limited basis. Trump was threatening to use a never-tested section of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act to impose his most recent Canada tariffs. (Other existing Canadian tariffs fall under yet another law.) What’s the big picture? This trade fight could preview an even bigger one to come, as the US, Mexico, and Canada attempt to renegotiate the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement that Trump struck in his first term. Trump declined to renew the deal last month, kicking off new negotiations. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. We got some incredibly good news about cancer treatment on Wednesday from the pharma companies Moderna and Merck, which announced a successful trial of an mRNA vaccine for melanoma , a particularly dangerous type of skin cancer. The idea of using vaccines — and specifically mRNA, which helped produce Covid vaccines in record time — to treat cancer isn’t new, but the Moderna and Merck trial is a big step on the path to getting a cancer vaccine approved by the FDA. As always, thanks for reading, and we’ll see you back here tomorrow! ##段落
政治 / 唐纳德·特朗普 / 《The Logoff》 加拿大新关税暂不征收——至少目前如此 很遗憾地告诉你，我们仍得考虑关税问题。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯，2026年8月19日，晚上10:15 UTC 赠阅 美国总统唐纳德·特朗普于2026年6月16日在法国埃维昂举行的七国集团峰会上与加拿大总理马克·卡尼交谈。图片来源：Evelyn Hockstein/AFP via Getty Images 卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的编辑人员。本文最初发表于《The Logoff》，这是一份每日通讯，帮助你了解特朗普政府动态，同时不让政治新闻占据你的全部生活。点击此处订阅。

##段落
欢迎来到《The Logoff》：美国总统唐纳德·特朗普计划对加拿大征收的关税已暂缓——至少目前如此。发生了什么？特朗普此前曾威胁对约200亿美元的加拿大商品征收50%的关税，但在周二深夜，即关税生效前几个小时，他推迟了这一措施。他在社交媒体帖子中写道，关税将“暂停三天，因为加拿大和美国，在文件最终敲定的前提下，已经达成协议！”

##段落
是否真的达成了协议？我们将在未来三天内见分晓。对特朗普的说法，我们始终应持保留态度。加拿大总理马克·卡尼仅表示，双方在达成协议方面取得了“实质性进展”，但“仍有重要工作要做”。周三，《华尔街日报》报道称，作为潜在贸易协议的一部分，美国可能降低此前对加拿大商品（涉及汽车、钢铁和铝）的关税。特朗普还暗示，协议可能使Keystone XL石油管道项目复活。

##段落
特朗普还能施加新关税吗？他可以。今年早些时候，最高法院推翻了特朗普利用《国际紧急经济权力法》这一特定法律征收关税的做法。此举终结了他的许多最广泛的关税措施，并剥夺了他最喜欢使用的征收手段。不过，他还有其他多种工具可以继续推进，尽管适用范围更为有限。特朗普曾威胁要利用1930年《斯姆特-霍利关税法》中一条从未被测试过的条款，来征收他对加拿大最新的关税。（其他现有的加拿大关税则依据另一项法律。）

##段落

readings.title: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
body: A smart way to handle anxiety — courtesy of soccer great Lionel Messi
What separates the very best in the world from the remaining 7 billion of us?

Exceptional talent often looks like an act of revolution — a person doing something in a way no one has ever done it before — but many revolutionary talents are actually built on a foundation of evolutionary tweaks. These tweaks develop over time, often compensating for weaknesses and anxieties that might derail a lesser talent.
For all his brilliance, though, Messi is famously anxious. For several years, he habitually vomited on the field before big matches.

Take the world’s best soccer player, an Argentinean named Lionel Messi. Messi has won more Ballon d’Or trophies, awarded to the best soccer player of the year, than any other player. He has scored more goals in a calendar year than any other living player, is the top all-time scorer in Spain’s La Liga, and has the highest goal ratio in the sport today, scoring almost once every match.

For all his brilliance, though, he’s famously anxious. For several years, Messi habitually vomited on the field before big matches. After a string of disappointing national-team losses, another former Argentinean giant of the game, the late Diego Maradona, uncharitably criticized Messi by suggesting that it was “useless trying to make a leader out of a man who goes to the toilet twenty times before a game.”

Being incredibly talented doesn’t immunize you against anxiety, and many of the world’s best grapple with anxiety precisely because they expect so much from themselves. But Messi hasn’t allowed his anxiety to diminish his brilliance because he’s mastered a coping mechanism that also doubles as the secret behind his tactical brilliance.
Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Second, he scopes out the opposition.

A soccer match runs for 90 minutes (plus a few minutes for “injury time”), and most players are active in the game from the first minute. As soon as the whistle blows, they implore their teammates to pass the ball and pursue the tactics their coaches laid out before the game.

But Messi is famous for not playing the game during its opening minutes. This is his evolutionary tweak, which developed as he played the game at progressively higher levels. For the opening minutes, Messi ambles back and forth near the middle of the field and almost never engages with his teammates. Whereas other players run and sometimes sprint, Messi spends much of his time walking, rarely breaking into more than a slow jog.

Messi does two things during these first few minutes. First, he calms himself. Easing into the game is Messi’s way of ensuring he’s fully engaged for the remainder of the game. His on-field vomiting has resolved itself, in part perhaps because he’s found a more effective way to calm his nerves. Second, he spends this time scoping out the opposition. His legs move slowly, but his eyes dart from player to player, assessing his opponents’ strengths, weaknesses, and tactics, and monitoring his own team’s movement with and around the ball. Messi is less valuable to his team early in the game, but this tactical pause elevates his value for the remaining 95 percent of the game.

If you split soccer game play into “preparatory” and “engaged” components, Messi leans heavily on preparation. During one classic game between Messi’s Barcelona and archrivals Real Madrid, in 2017, Messi ran for just four minutes and walked for more than eighty of the game’s ninety minutes. When he was engaged, though, he was dynamic, creating nine chances, scoring one goal, and feeding the ball to a teammate who scored another goal.
As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act.

That pattern isn’t unusual for Messi, and it’s often in the biggest games that he accentuates his in-game preparation. That preparation also explains his ability to find himself in the right place at the right time, over and over. Though his positional play appears otherworldly, it isn’t a miracle; it’s that he’s learned, minute by minute, that a particular defender leaves a particular square of pitch uncovered or that two midfielders leave a small corner of the pitch open when they gravitate to the middle of the field.
The lesson for the rest of us is clear: When you’re anxious, whether in athletics or in life more broadly, pause. Slow down . Prepare.

As you might imagine, pausing is harder than it sounds. In the face of silence and anxiety, our instinct is to act. Judson Brewer, a psychiatrist and neuroscientist, has spent much of his career thinking about how to do nothing.
About fifteen years ago, Brewer developed a mindfulness-based treatment for addiction.
His approach instructs addicts to resist the waves of anxiety during moments of craving by following the four steps of an approach that goes by the acronym RAIN:
I nvestigate your emotions and thoughts (e.g., “What is happening in my body now?”)
N ote what is happening from moment to moment.

Brewer has said that his approach was inspired by clinical psychologist Tara Brach’s . To test the approach, Brewer worked with smokers who were struggling to quit. Nicotine addiction is notoriously stubborn — more so than many harder drugs that produce stronger immediate responses in users.

Before unleashing the program on smokers, Brewer wanted to test the system on himself. The problem was “I was a nonsmoker,” Brewer wrote, “who needed to be able to relate to patients who felt as though their heads were going to explode unless they smoked.”

Nicotine has a half-life of around two hours, so to begin, smokers need to resist the urge to light up for two hours at a time. Brewer reasoned that smokers who could last two hours without a cigarette would cultivate new nonsmoking habits, extending those stretches till they no longer felt the urge to smoke at all.

He simulated these periods of resistance by learning to meditate for two-hour stretches without moving. During moments of restlessness, he followed the RAIN steps — recognize, allow, investigate, note — and if he moved his body, the clock would reset, and he’d have to start again.

This might sound easy, but two hours is a long time to sit still without entertainment. “Surprisingly it wasn’t the physical pain of not shifting for a long time that got me,” Brewer wrote. “It was the restlessness … Those cravings shouted, ‘Get up!’ ”
Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean.

For many months, Brewer would get close, then restlessness would defeat him. “Then one day,” he wrote, “I did it. I sat for the full two hours … Each subsequent sit got easier and easier because I had the confidence that it could be done. And I knew that my patients could quit smoking. They simply needed the proper tools.”

Brewer was right. His patients had been stuck, incapable of quitting one of the most addictive substances on earth. But when he ran study after study, pitting his RAIN mindfulness method against the most effective addiction treatment approaches of the day, his approach was more than twice as effective.

Months later, when most of the patients on other treatment plans had relapsed, his mindfulness group stayed clean. They were more than five times as likely to have shaken their addictions using an approach that essentially taught them to pause at the moment their bodies were most urgently driving them to act.

Of the four steps in Brewer’s RAIN approach, the second — allowing — is perhaps the most critical. Allowing an experience to wash over you sounds disarmingly easy because it doesn’t require you to do anything. But that’s exactly the point. It’s difficult because you’re forced to do nothing despite the urge to act.

一个应对焦虑的聪明办法——来自足球巨星莱昂内尔·梅西
2023年6月22日
/
亚当·阿尔特博士

德博拉·斯皮尔曼

是什么将世界顶尖人物与其余70亿人区分开来？
非凡天赋往往看起来像一场革命——一个人以从未有人用过的方式做事——但许多革命性天赋实际上建立在渐进式微调的基础上。这些微调随着时间发展，常常弥补那些可能会击垮较弱天赋的弱点和焦虑。

尽管才华横溢，但梅西以焦虑著称。多年来，他在重大比赛前习惯性地在球场上呕吐。

以世界最佳足球运动员、阿根廷人莱昂内尔·梅西为例。梅西获得的金球奖（授予年度最佳足球运动员）比任何其他球员都多。他在一个日历年内的进球数超过任何在世球员，是西班牙西甲联赛历史最佳射手，并且拥有当今足球界最高的进球率，几乎每场比赛都能进球。

尽管才华横溢，但他以焦虑闻名。多年来，梅西在大赛前习惯性地在球场上呕吐。在一连串令人失望的国家队失利后，另一位已故的阿根廷足球巨匠迭戈·马拉多纳不客气地批评梅西，暗示“试图把一个赛前上二十次厕所的人培养成领袖是徒劳的”。

拥有惊人的天赋并不能让你免受焦虑的侵扰，而世界上许多顶尖人物恰恰因为对自己期望过高而深陷焦虑。但梅西没有让焦虑削弱他的才华，因为他掌握了一种应对机制，这种机制同时也正是他战术智慧背后的秘密。

梅西在这最初的几分钟里做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。第二，他观察对手。

一场足球比赛持续90分钟（外加几分钟“伤停补时”），大多数球员从第一分钟起就积极投入比赛。哨声一响，他们就恳求队友传球，并执行教练赛前布置的战术。

但梅西以在开场几分钟不参与比赛而闻名。这是他的渐进式微调，是他在越来越高的水平上踢球时逐渐发展出来的。在开场几分钟里，梅西在中场附近来回踱步，几乎不与队友互动。其他球员在奔跑，有时甚至冲刺，而梅西大部分时间在走路，很少超过慢跑的速度。

梅西在这最初的几分钟里做两件事。第一，他让自己冷静下来。慢慢融入比赛是梅

ssi确保自己在比赛剩余时间内完全投入的方式。他在场上呕吐的问题已经自行解决，部分原因可能是他找到了更有效的镇定神经的方法。其次，他利用这段时间观察对手。他的双腿移动缓慢，但目光却从一名球员迅速扫向另一名球员，评估对手的优势、劣势和战术，同时监控己方球队在持球和无球时的跑动。梅西在比赛初期对球队的价值较低，但这种战术性的停顿提升了他在剩余95%比赛时间里的价值。

如果你将足球比赛分为“准备”和“投入”两个部分，梅西则严重偏向于准备。在2017年梅西所在的巴塞罗那对阵宿敌皇家马德里的一场经典比赛中，梅西只跑了四分钟，而在九十分钟的比赛中有八十多分钟是在走路。然而，当他投入时，他充满活力，创造了九次机会，打入一球，并助攻队友再进一球。

正如你可能想象的，停顿比听起来要难得多。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。

这种模式对梅西来说并不罕见，而且往往在最重要的比赛中，他会强化自己的赛前准备。这种准备也解释了他在正确的时间出现在正确地点的能力，并且屡试不爽。尽管他的位置感看起来超凡脱俗，但这并非奇迹；而是他每分钟都在学习，比如某个后卫会留下某块球场区域无人防守，或者两名中场球员向中路靠拢时会暴露出球场的一小角。

对我们其他人的教训很明确：当你感到焦虑时，无论是在体育竞技还是更广泛的生活中，都要停顿。放慢脚步。做好准备。

正如你可能想象的，停顿比听起来要难得多。面对沉默和焦虑，我们的本能是行动。贾德森·布鲁尔，一位精神病学家和神经科学家，职业生涯的大部分时间都在思考如何“什么都不做”。

大约十五年前，布鲁尔开发了一种基于正念的成瘾治疗方法。

他的方法指导成瘾者在渴望来袭时，通过遵循一个缩写为RAIN的四步法来抵抗焦虑的浪潮：

R——识别正在升起的感受。
A——允许它存在。
I——探究你的情绪和想法（例如，“我身体里现在发生了什么？”）
N——时刻觉察正在发生的一切。

布鲁尔曾表示，他的方法受到临床心理学家塔拉·布拉赫的启发。为了测试这种方法，布鲁尔与努力戒烟的吸烟者合作。尼古丁成瘾以顽固著称——比许多能产生更强烈即时反应的硬性毒品更难戒除。

在将该项目推广之前

在吸烟者身上，布鲁尔想在自己身上测试这套系统。问题在于“我不是吸烟者，”布鲁尔写道，“但我需要能理解那些觉得不抽烟脑袋就要爆炸的患者。”

尼古丁的半衰期大约为两小时，因此开始时，吸烟者需要每次抵抗吸烟冲动两小时。布鲁尔推断，能坚持两小时不吸烟的人会培养出新的非吸烟习惯，逐步延长这些时段，直到完全不再感到吸烟冲动。

他通过练习冥想两小时不动来模拟这些抵抗期。在不安的时刻，他遵循RAIN步骤——识别、允许、探究、注意——如果他移动身体，计时器就会重置，他得重新开始。

这听起来可能容易，但静坐两小时且不娱乐其实很长。“令人惊讶的是，长时间不动并非身体疼痛让我难受，”布鲁尔写道，“而是那种不安……那些渴求在喊‘起来！’”

几个月后，当其他治疗计划中的大多数患者复发时，他的正念小组保持清醒。

许多个月里，布鲁尔接近成功，但不安总会击败他。“然后有一天，”他写道，“我做到了。我坐满了整整两小时……每次后续静坐越来越容易，因为我有信心能做到。我也知道我的患者能戒烟。他们只需要合适的工具。”

布鲁尔是对的。他的患者曾困在无法戒掉地球上最易上瘾物质的境地。但当他进行一项项研究，将他的RAIN正念方法与当时最有效的成瘾治疗方法对比时，他的方法效果是两倍以上。

几个月后，当其他治疗计划中的大多数患者复发时，他的正念小组保持清醒。他们用这种方法戒除成瘾的可能性是其他方法的五倍以上，这种方法本质上是教他们在身体最急切驱使他们行动时暂停。

在布鲁尔RAIN方法的四个步骤中，第二步——允许——或许最为关键。允许一种体验冲刷过你听起来简单得令人放松，因为它不要求你做任何事。但这正是重点。它之所以困难，是因为尽管有行动的冲动，你却被迫什么都不做。

尽管暂停和准备有诸多好处，但有时主要事件并不按计划进行。梅西输过无数场比赛，而布鲁尔的尼古丁成瘾者并非都在实验结束数周或数月后保持戒断。掌握这些失败后的焦虑和不适至关重要，这是其中的关键之一。

那些取得突破性成就的人与长期陷入困境的人之间的关键差异。

readings.title: The Trump-Kim Jong Un bromance comes roaring back
body: Today, Explained newsletter The Trump-Kim Jong Un bromance comes roaring back A new test for the US-South Korea relationship as Trump curtails joint military exercises. by Cameron Peters Aug 17, 2026, 10:25 PM UTC Gift President Donald Trump gives a thumbs up before boarding Air Force One in Cleveland, Ohio, on August 11, 2026. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here . Hi readers, it’s me again! Caitlin will be back on Wednesday. Now, for today’s news: President Donald Trump, South Korea, and the state of the US’s military alliances. Remember Trump’s first-term “ love letters ” with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un? Trump was so fond of them that he took them with him when he left the presidency in 2021 (the National Archives did not approve ). Now, it seems like the two leaders are taking up where they left off. Over the weekend, Trump announced in a social media post that he would “substantially reduce” scheduled joint military exercises between the US and South Korea, which get underway today. The reason? His “very good relationship with Kim Jong Un, of North Korea.” But there may have been another reason. Trump also wrote that “While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, “No thanks!”” The US-South Korea exercises “are not only costly, with much of these costs paid for by the United States of America (as usual!),” Trump wrote, “but send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful.” That last part — “unthreatening and respectful” — is not exactly true; in 2017, Kim called Trump “a mentally deranged US dotard” whom North Korea would “tame…with fire.” But in the present day, Trump’s announcement is a boon to the North Korean leader, who has denounced the military exercises. It’s also just the latest incident in the historically close US-South Korea relationship (the two countries have held military exercises annually for more than 70 years). Earlier this year, Trump lashed out with new tariffs , accusing South Korea of “not living up to its Deal,” referring to a 2025 agreement on trade and security between the two countries that South Korea’s legislature had not yet approved. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. The US has more permanent troops in South Korea than it does almost anywhere else in the world, behind only its deployments in Japan and Germany. Under Trump, though, those once-durable commitments have started to look a lot shakier. Europe — and Germany in particular — has borne the brunt of Trump’s second-term harassment: In May, Trump announced his intent to remove 5,000 US troops from Germany and threatened to go “a lot further”; the Pentagon has said that withdrawal will take place within 12 months . The US currently has more than 38,000 troops stationed in Germany. Trump has made similar threats about US troops stationed in Italy and Spain , and even suggested removing all US troops from Europe. Most of these threats have been triggered by Trump’s unhappiness with European defense spending , which he’s eternally trying to boost. But in his second term, the threats have grown much more tightly tied to Trump’s personal ambitions and grievances. Trump’s Germany announcement followed a clash with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz over the US war with Iran, which Trump has tried — unsuccessfully — to drag US allies into . Spain , in particular, has also drawn Trump’s ire for vocally opposing the war. Last month, he also tied the US troop presence in Europe to his insistence that the US be allowed to take over Greenland, which belongs to Denmark, a US ally and founding NATO member. ➨ A low-tech way to save coral reefs. My colleague Benji Jones visited the island nation of Palau, in the western Pacific Ocean, to learn about a new approach to reef restoration . Scientists there are testing species of coral specifically for heat resistance to find better options for replanting reefs — all using some plastic picnic coolers and a bit of hot water. Did you know… that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in the Chilean Andes has the largest digital camera ever made? It captured its “first light” last year in staggering high-definition. Today’s trivia: What was the title of Iran’s ruler until 1979? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword . Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Friday’s trivia: On Friday, we asked you which US president responded to inflation by ordering wage and price freezes. That was President Richard Nixon. ##段落
《今日解说》通讯稿：特朗普与金正恩的“兄弟情”卷土重来。美国缩减联合军演，为美韩关系带来新考验。作者：卡梅伦·彼得斯，2026年8月17日，晚上10:25（UTC）。

##段落
赠品：2026年8月11日，总统唐纳德·特朗普在俄亥俄州克利夫兰登上空军一号前竖起大拇指。吉姆·沃森/法新社 via 盖蒂图片社。卡梅伦·彼得斯是Vox的编辑。本文曾刊登于《今日解说》，这是一份每日通讯，帮你理解当天最引人注目的新闻和故事。点击此处订阅。

##段落
读者们好，又是我！凯特琳周三回归。现在来看今天的新闻：唐纳德·特朗普总统、韩国，以及美国军事同盟的现状。还记得特朗普第一任期时与朝鲜独裁者金正恩的“情书”往来吗？特朗普对此情有独钟，2021年卸任时甚至带走了这些信件（国家档案馆可没批准）。如今，两位领导人似乎又续上了前缘。

##段落
上周末，特朗普在社交媒体发帖宣布，将“大幅削减”美韩原定的联合军事演习——这些演习今天启动。原因何在？因为他与“朝鲜的金正恩关系非常好”。但或许还有另一层原因。特朗普还写道：“虽然有点不相关（？），但我最近问韩国总统，是否愿意加入我们对伊朗伊斯兰共和国的无核化行动，他们回答：‘不了，谢谢！’”特朗普称，美韩军演“不仅代价高昂，其中大部分费用由美利坚合众国承担（照旧！），而且向一个国家发出了完全不恰当且充满敌意的信号——只要唐纳德·J·特朗普担任总统，这个国家就一直是不具威胁且尊重的。”

##段落
最后那句——“不具威胁且尊重”——并不完全属实；2017年，金正恩曾称特朗普为“精神错乱的美国老糊涂”，并扬言要用“烈火”来“驯服”他。但就当下而言，特朗普的宣布对这位朝鲜领导人来说是一大利好，后者一直谴责这些军事演习。这也只是美韩关系史上最新的一起事件——两国举行联合军演已超过70年。今年早些时候，特朗普曾以新关税发难，指责韩国“没有履行协议”，指的是两国2025年达成的一项贸易与安全协议，而韩国立法机构尚未批准该协议。

##段落
邮箱（必填）提交。提交即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。美国在韩国的常驻军队数量，几乎超过其在任何其他国家的驻军。

在世界其他地方，美国驻军规模仅次于日本和德国。然而，在特朗普的领导下，这些曾经稳固的承诺已开始显得岌岌可危。欧洲——尤其是德国——承受了特朗普第二任期内的主要压力：5月，特朗普宣布计划从德国撤出5000名美军，并威胁要“更进一步”；五角大楼表示撤军将在12个月内完成。目前，美国在德国驻扎了超过3.8万名士兵。特朗普还对驻意大利和西班牙的美军发出了类似威胁，甚至建议从欧洲撤出所有美军。这些威胁大多源于特朗普对欧洲防务开支的不满，他一直试图推动欧洲增加军费。但在第二任期内，这些威胁与特朗普的个人野心和不满情绪联系得更加紧密。特朗普宣布对德国的撤军决定，之前他与德国总理弗里德里希·默茨就美国对伊朗的战争发生冲突，特朗普试图拉拢盟友参战但未成功。尤其是西班牙，因其公开反对战争而激怒了特朗普。上个月，他还将美国在欧洲的驻军与坚持允许美国接管格陵兰岛挂钩，该岛属于丹麦，而丹麦是美国盟友和北约创始成员国。

➨ 一种低科技方法来拯救珊瑚礁。我的同事本吉·琼斯访问了西太平洋的帕劳岛国，了解了一种新的珊瑚礁修复方法。那里的科学家正在测试特定种类的珊瑚，以筛选耐热品种，为重新种植珊瑚礁寻找更优选择——全部使用一些塑料野餐冷却器和一点热水。

你知道吗……位于智利安第斯山脉的维拉·鲁宾天文台拥有有史以来最大的数码相机？它去年以惊人的高清画质捕捉到了“第一缕光”。今日冷知识：伊朗的统治者直到1979年拥有什么头衔？（你可以在Vox的每日填字游戏中找到这个及其他脑力谜题。答案见明日版。）周五冷知识：周五，我们问你哪位美国总统通过下令冻结工资和物价来应对通货膨胀。答案是理查德·尼克松总统。

readings.title: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
body: 3 strategies for effective leadership, from a former astronaut
" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> Maria Petrishina / iStock

While there are various approaches to leading a team, many of us land on common questions in the search for an effective leadership style: How can I be there for my team? Do I need to command respect, or earn it? And the most crucial question of all: How can I make sure that my team trusts me?

Cady Coleman has been confronting these questions throughout her career as a chemist, engineer, Air Force colonel and astronaut. In conversation with TED science curator David Biello, Coleman shared three strategies to establish — and maintain — trust in a leader. Whatever your career is, these tips can help you to prepare your team to face any challenge you come across — in outer space or here on Earth.
People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team” … But maybe there should be.
1. Be brave enough to get to know your team members as individuals

People often say, “There’s no ‘I’ in team”… But maybe there should be, says Coleman. Every member of your team is a whole person, and since so many of the problems we face at work are interdisciplinary, understanding who each individual is beyond the 9-to-5 is valuable. Being vulnerable enough to get to know your team this way is an essential skill for any leader.

When you are able to say, “I think your world is different from mine, and I’d like to understand more about it,” you’re not just building trust; you’re opening a communication channel that teaches you more about your teammate’s qualities, says Coleman. This type of conversation requires the willingness and bravery to be vulnerable. Once you know what everyone brings to the table, you can foster the growth of qualities that can lead the team to collective success.

For example, as Coleman prepared for life on the space station, her advisors warned that the long periods of time away from family might be too much to handle. For her, however, this wasn’t a problem — she had been commuting and working away from her family for more than a decade. After sharing her experience, her colleagues realized she’d not only be adaptable to life on the space station, but also she could help others cope with the change, too.
2. Create a culture that’s open to everyone’s ideas
While leaders have to guide their teams, it’s equally important to let everyone know that they can advocate for themselves and bring their own ideas to the table.

Coleman benefitted from such leadership at NASA when she was training to go to the space station. In the face of budget cuts, NASA announced that they’d be eliminating their smaller space suits, meaning that if someone wasn’t qualified to use a larger space suit, they couldn’t go to the space station. This presented a choice for Coleman: wait for NASA to acquire suits that fit her or figure out how she could train in the larger suits. By working with NASA’s decision makers, Coleman was able to shift her training to use the bigger suits. Had she not felt the freedom to speak up, she says, she would have been waiting 10 years to go to the space station in a small suit.
When you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily.

Sometimes establishing trust in the workplace can be more difficult than you expect, but when you make trust-building a central goal, the rest falls into place more easily. Workplace dynamics are always changing — maybe a teammate’s work/life priorities have shifted, or a big mistake requires you all to work together under new pressures. These challenges make fostering trust tricky, but they are also moments of opportunity.

If a new challenge has arisen or trust has been breached, Coleman reminds us to “always figure out the why and the what.” Make sure to ask: why has this happened, why do they feel this way, and what can be done about it? Be open to different points of view, and don’t give up if you don’t get through at first. Connection is often in the smaller things you do; talk about food or music, write a note to compliment an idea and ask to hear more. This level of connection and vulnerability may not seem intuitive at first, but as you make trust a core part of your mission, it becomes easy.

Trust, Coleman reminds us, is both given and earned. As a woman, she knew gaining the trust of some male colleagues might be extra challenging. Her approach was simple: she performed well and, with patience and persistence, learned her colleagues’ language and taught them hers. The challenges in gaining trust will always be there, but if you model vulnerability, openness and understanding for your team, you’ll find the rewards will always be there, too.

This post was adapted from a recent LinkedIn Live conversation with Cady Coleman, former NASA Astronaut and author of the forthcoming book, Sharing Space: An Astronaut’s Guide to Mission, Wonder, and Making Change , due out July 2024.

" data-large-file="https://ideas.ted.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2023/11/IDEAS_Leadership_FINAL.jpg?w=770" /> 玛丽亚·佩特里希娜 / iStock
领导力是什么样子？
虽然带领团队的方式多种多样，但许多人在寻找有效领导风格时都会遇到一些常见问题：我该如何支持我的团队？我需要命令别人尊重，还是赢得尊重？而最关键的问题是：我如何确保我的团队信任我？
凯迪·科尔曼在她的职业生涯中一直面对这些问题，她曾担任化学家、工程师、空军上校和宇航员。在与TED科学策展人大卫·比埃洛的对话中，科尔曼分享了建立并维持领导者信任的三个策略。无论你的职业是什么，这些建议都能帮助你让团队准备好面对你遇到的任何挑战——无论是在外太空还是在地球上。
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有。
1. 勇敢地去了解你的团队成员作为个体
人们常说，“团队里没有‘我’”……但也许应该有，科尔曼说。你的每个团队成员都是一个完整的人，而且由于我们在工作中遇到的许多问题都是跨学科的，了解每个人在朝九晚五之外是谁是很有价值的。以足够脆弱的心态去这样了解你的团队，是任何领导者的基本技能。
当你能说“我觉得你的世界和我的不同，我想多了解一些”时，你不只是在建立信任；你还在打开一条沟通渠道，让你更了解队友的特质，科尔曼说。这种对话需要愿意和勇气去展现脆弱。一旦你知道每个人能带来什么，你就能培养那些能带领团队走向集体成功的特质。
例如，当科尔曼为空间站生活做准备时，她的顾问警告说长时间远离家人可能难以承受。然而对她来说，这不是问题——她已经通勤并在离家之外工作十多年了。分享她的经历后，同事们意识到她不仅能适应空间站的生活，还能帮助其他人应对这种变化。
2. 创造一种对每个人的想法都开放的文化
虽然领导者必须引导团队，但同样重要的是让每个人知道他们可以为自己发声，并把自己的想法带到桌面上。
科尔曼在NASA训练时受益于这种领导方式，当时她正在为前往太空做准备。

面对预算削减，NASA宣布将淘汰较小尺寸的太空服，这意味着如果某人不符合使用较大太空服的条件，就无法前往空间站。这对科尔曼来说是一个选择：等待NASA获得适合她的太空服，或者想办法训练自己使用较大的太空服。通过与NASA的决策者合作，科尔曼得以调整训练，改用较大的太空服。她说，如果她没有感到可以自由发声，她可能要等上10年才能穿着小号太空服前往空间站。

当你将建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。

3. 将信任作为你的使命

有时在工作场所建立信任可能比你预期的更困难，但当你将建立信任作为核心目标时，其他事情就会更容易水到渠成。职场动态总是在变化——也许队友的工作与生活优先级发生了转变，或者一次重大失误要求你们在新的压力下共同协作。这些挑战使培养信任变得棘手，但同时也是机遇的时刻。

如果出现了新的挑战或信任被破坏，科尔曼提醒我们要“始终弄清楚原因和内容”。务必询问：为什么会发生这种情况，他们为什么有这样的感受，以及能对此做些什么？对不同观点保持开放态度，如果一开始没有取得进展，不要放弃。联系往往体现在你做的细小事情中；谈论食物或音乐，写便条赞美一个想法并请求了解更多。这种程度的联系和坦诚起初可能看起来不直观，但当你将信任作为使命的核心部分时，它就会变得容易。

科尔曼提醒我们，信任既是给予的，也是赢得的。作为一名女性，她知道获得一些男性同事的信任可能格外具有挑战性。她的方法很简单：她表现出色，并以耐心和坚持，学会了同事们的语言，同时也教会了他们自己的语言。赢得信任的挑战始终存在，但如果你为团队树立坦诚、开放和理解的榜样，你会发现回报也始终存在。

本文改编自最近与凯迪·科尔曼的LinkedIn Live对话，她是前NASA宇航员，即将出版的著作《共享太空：宇航员的任务、奇迹与变革指南》定于2024年7月发行。

在此观看完整的LinkedIn对话：

来自我们的合作伙伴美国空军的消息：美国空军的使命是飞行、战斗和取胜——随时随地提供空中力量。无论是全职、兼职，还是穿制服或不穿制服，每个服役人员都在帮助我们实现任务成功中扮演着关键角色。

readings.title: Should you spend your money on retirement or give it to your kids?
body: Future Perfect Should you spend your money on retirement or give it to your kids? ﻿The secret to a more enriching retirement may start with abandoning your zero-sum thinking. by Shayla Love Aug 16, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Gift How can you reap what you sow while sharing with your descendants too? ﻿Pete Gamlen for Vox Shayla Love is a science journalist based in Brooklyn who writes about science, health, and the mind. Hi readers! Shayla Love here, science journalist and longtime fan of Your Mileage May Vary. I’m honored to be subbing for Sigal Samuel while she’s out on parental leave. I’m diving into your questions as a way to help understand human nature and our choices through multiple lenses: philosophical, psychological, and beyond. Please send in any emotional, body/brain, sociological, perceptual, or other kind of life quandaries you might have. I am a (gracefully?) aging mother of three and proud grandmother of four. I keep hearing about how my generation (okay, I am a boomer) is hoarding wealth and failing to pass it down. When I look at my lifestyle, I’m facing a fork in the road. Either I splurge on a lovely retirement, or I save so my kids and their kids can have an easier life. We’re all middle-class, so this is not a question of survival. The kids have college funds. Do I owe it to my descendants to scrimp as I age? Surely it’s not right for me to spend my savings on bucket-list vacations…How should I balance spending on myself and on the others that will come after me? Dear Rainy Day Funder, I’m so glad to hear you’re not in financial survival mode. But you are facing some economic constraints : You can’t splurge on a luxurious retirement while at the same time saving a substantial nest egg for your kids and grandkids. Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here! It sounds like this feeling of either-or is causing you some anguish. The instinctual response is, as you suggest, to hoard as much as possible for your progeny to use later on. But at the same time, that feels like it’s zero-summing your own experience in your golden years. So I’d like to introduce you to an economic thinker who has some advice that might surprise you. John Maynard Keynes, 19th-century British economist, would say: Don’t save your money! Keynes wrote that when times are tough, people react by keeping their money close, and not spending it. But this sets in motion what he called the paradox of thrift . One person’s expenses are actually another person’s income, he pointed out; if everyone saved their money, no one would make money either, and a recession could drag on and on. In the end, people’s savings would, paradoxically, go down, even though they were scrimping. We can apply the paradox of thrift to your own family as a mini-economy. Inheritance has traditionally worked by setting aside large chunks of your assets to pass along to your children and grandchildren — which could be helpful when the day of windfall comes. But why wait? And would waiting actually stymie your family’s financial potential? In past generations, an inheritance like this often happened far earlier. I’m comforted that we are living longer (an average of a decade or more longer) than in the mid-20th century, but this sets up new issues, as you’re stuck in, with when and in what quantity to transfer any extra resources. Now, as people retire with decades of good life to enjoy ahead of them, they are often doing so at the very same time their adult children are the most financially stressed: They are trying to buy homes, they’re in the busiest middle part of their careers, and many have children of their own they’re raising and trying to save for. This doesn’t mean you have to give away all your money to your family so that they can spend it on the pleasures you have given up. Keynes wasn’t anti-savings so that money could be spent frivolously. He did believe that spending money was one of the best ways to give the greater economy a boost. Perhaps there are ways you could think about spending your money that stimulate your family’s internal economy, that also help you enjoy your retirement. For example, you could invest in a lakeside property to kick your feet up at — an asset that will appreciate in value over time and be sold at a profit, or be passed down through the generations to enjoy for many summers to come. Maybe you assist your children in buying a home — one with a comfortable guest suite. You could invest in a business your children want to start, and help them grow something that could accrue more wealth over time. Using your money these ways may even feel more like splurging than scrimping! Yet, it ideally would achieve both: a fun way to spend your hard-earned money now, and create more abundance for your family’s future. A hidden bonus of non-traditional inheritance moves like these is that they all involve spending more time together with your family and potentially even strengthening those relationships along the way. The Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote in The Nicomachean Ethics that there were three kinds of friends. Some are based on utility, and exist only because of what people can get from one another. Other friendships are based on pleasure, when you like doing things with someone. Finally, friendships of virtue persist because you stick by people who inspire you by their strong character. Simply setting aside your money is a relationship that leans utilitarian. Working on a shared meaningful project could help deepen your relationships with your kids and grandkids in those pleasurable and virtuous directions. Speaking of, I don’t think you need to be making these decisions alone. You used an interesting word in your question: Do you, as an individual, owe it to your family to set them up with a more comfortable financial future, at the expense of personal indulgences? A lot of the discussion around older generations’ money, and whether or how they should pass it on, avoids dealing with this sticky moral component. Why should parents give their kids money? I think there’s clarity to be found in thinking more closely about why we owe each other anything. There are few better thinkers to turn to than Confucius to consider our obligations to family. The fifth-century Chinese philosopher believed that we can’t understand ourselves only as individuals . You are nobody when you are alone; you only come alive as a mother, a daughter, or a sister. These relational roles each come with specific duties and ways of interacting. Successfully fulfilling these roles within the family has a bigger impact, according to Confucius. It’s what creates the foundations for a harmonious and functional society. For children in this web of relations, it’s critical to uphold filial piety, or the need to respect, honor, and care for parents as well as all of their other elders and ancestors. Filial piety has, over the years, been criticized for being too rigid, and setting overly high expectations for blind obedience and conformity in children. So I’ve been interested to see the concept of reciprocal filial piety emerge. In reciprocal filial piety, children have a genuine feeling of gratitude to their parents for raising them, and any obligation they feel is heartfelt — they want to return the favor and care for their parents too. As a half-Chinese person, I find it interesting that in family life in the West, filial piety is often reversed. There’s a lot of air time discussing what parents owe their children, and not so much the other way around. For example, I noticed that you don’t mention how your family intends to care for you in the future, or what they might feel a sense of owing you. If you do take a Keynesian approach to your family and decide to spend your money in ways that could benefit everyone, it might be worth engaging in some Confucian-tinted conversations not only about what you owe everyone else, but what you all appreciate about each other. You can reflect, together, on how your family is stronger because of all the ways you’ve chosen to look after one another, not only because of how much money is in the bank. I think it’s worth having a copy of The Analects of Confucius lying around, which is full of nuggets of wisdom. One morsel I recently read was about how to best get along with others: “The gentleman harmonizes without being an echo. The petty man echoes and does not harmonize.” The lesson is that we don’t gain much by blindly following and copying what other people do. The most harmonious way to be in a society, or even a family, is to have interlocking roles that complement each other, like different pitches do in a choir. I thought a lot about getting older when reading this piece on death doulas by Alexandra Schwartz in The New Yorker. It serves as a reminder that people outside of the immediate family can also help with life’s hardest transitions. And, for something fun: I enjoyed this investigation by Natalie Wolchover in Quanta on why she (or anyone) is left-handed. She explores left-handed stigma and neuroscience, as well as a theory about humans using their right hands because they once were better to win fights with. 未来完成时 你应该把钱花在退休生活上，还是留给孩子们？丰富退休生活的秘诀，或许始于摒弃你的零和思维。作者：Shayla Love 2026年8月16日，下午12:00 UTC 赠阅 如何在与后代分享的同时，也能收获自己播种的果实？Pete Gamlen为Vox供图 Shayla Love是驻布鲁克林的科学记者，撰写关于科学、健康和心智的文章。读者们好！我是Shayla Love，科学记者，也是《你的里程可能不同》的长期粉丝。我很荣幸能在Sigal Samuel休产假期间代笔。我深入探讨你们的问题，旨在通过哲学、心理学等多重视角帮助理解人性和我们的选择。请把你们可能遇到的情感、身体/大脑、社会学、感知或其他类型的人生困惑发给我。我是一个（优雅地？）老去的三个孩子的母亲，也是四个孙辈的骄傲祖母。我不断听到人们说我这一代人（好吧，我是婴儿潮一代）在囤积财富，没有把它传下去。当我审视自己的生活方式时，我正面临一个岔路口。要么我挥霍享受一个美好的退休生活，要么我存钱让我的孩子和他们的孩子过上更轻松的生活。我们都是中产阶级，所以这不是生存问题。孩子们有大学基金。我是否欠后代一笔账，应该在年老时省吃俭用？当然，把我的积蓄花在遗愿清单式的旅行上似乎不对……我该如何平衡花在自己身上和花在后来者身上？

##段落

亲爱的雨天储蓄者，我很高兴听到你不在财务生存模式中。但你确实面临一些经济约束：你不能一边挥霍奢华的退休生活，一边为你的孩子和孙辈存下一大笔储备金。填写这份匿名表格！订阅通讯的读者将比其他人都先看到我的专栏，他们的问题将在未来版本中优先处理。点击这里订阅！听起来这种非此即彼的感觉正在让你痛苦。正如你所说，本能的反应是尽可能多地囤积，留给后代以后使用。但同时，这感觉像是在让你的黄金岁月变成零和游戏。所以我想向你介绍一位经济思想家，他有一些建议可能会让你惊讶。19世纪英国经济学家约翰·梅纳德·凯恩斯会说：别存钱！凯恩斯写道，当形势艰难时，人们的反应是把钱攥在手里，不去花。但这引发了他所谓的“节俭悖论”。他指出，一个人的支出实际上是另一个人的收入；如果每个人都存钱，那谁也没法赚钱，经济衰退可能会无限期拖下去。最终，悖论性地，人们的储蓄反而会下降，即使

尽管他们一直在省吃俭用。我们可以将“节俭悖论”应用到你的家庭这个小经济体上。传统上，遗产的运作方式是留出一大块资产传给子女和孙辈——这在天降横财的那一天到来时可能会有所帮助。但为什么要等呢？而且，等待是否会反而阻碍你家庭的财务潜力？在过去的几代人中，这样的遗产往往发生得更早。让我感到欣慰的是，我们比20世纪中叶的人活得更长（平均多出十年或更久），但这带来了新的问题，因为你被困在何时以及以何种数量转移任何多余资源的困境中。如今，人们退休时还有几十年的美好生活在前方等着他们，而往往正是在这个时候，他们的成年子女正面临最大的经济压力：他们试图买房，正处于职业生涯最忙碌的中段，许多人还有自己的孩子要抚养并努力储蓄。这并不意味着你必须把所有的钱都送给家人，让他们花在你已放弃的享乐上。凯恩斯并不反对储蓄，以便钱能被挥霍掉。他确实相信，花钱是提振整体经济的最佳方式之一。也许有一些方式可以让你思考如何花钱，既能刺激家庭内部经济，又能帮助你享受退休生活。例如，你可以投资一处湖畔房产，供你放松休憩——这是一项会随时间增值的资产，将来可以出售获利，或者代代相传，供未来许多夏天享用。也许你可以帮助子女买房——一栋带有舒适客房套间的房子。你可以投资子女想创业的项目，帮助他们发展出随时间积累更多财富的事业。以这些方式使用你的钱，甚至可能让你感觉更像是在挥霍，而不是在节俭！然而，理想情况下，这能实现两个目标：现在以一种有趣的方式花掉你辛苦赚来的钱，同时为家庭的未来创造更多富足。像这样的非传统遗产举措的一个隐藏好处是，它们都涉及与家人共度更多时光，并可能在此过程中加强这些关系。希腊哲学家亚里士多德在《尼各马可伦理学》中写道，有三种朋友。有些基于功利，只因人们能互相获取而存在。其他友谊基于愉悦，当你喜欢和某人一起做事时。最后，德性友谊之所以持久，是因为你支持那些以坚强品格激励你的人。单纯地存钱是一种偏向功利性的关系。共同追求一个有意义的共同目标，则能建立更深厚的联系。

一个有意义的事业能帮助你与子女和孙辈在愉悦和向善的方向上加深关系。说到这，我认为你不必独自做出这些决定。你在问题中用一个有趣的词：作为个体，你是否亏欠家庭，让他们拥有更舒适的财务未来，而牺牲个人享乐？关于老一辈金钱的讨论，以及他们是否或如何传递财富，往往回避了这种棘手的道德成分。为什么父母要给子女钱？我认为，更仔细地思考我们为何彼此亏欠，能带来清晰的认识。要探讨我们对家庭的责任，没有比孔子更好的思想家了。这位五世纪的中国哲学家认为，我们不能只把自己理解为个体。独处时你谁都不是；你只有作为母亲、女儿或姐妹时才鲜活起来。这些关系角色各有特定职责和互动方式。孔子认为，在家庭中成功履行这些角色影响更大，这是和谐、功能健全社会的基础。在这种关系网络中的子女，遵守孝道至关重要，即尊重、敬爱并照顾父母以及所有长辈和祖先。多年来，孝道因过于僵化，且对子女的盲从和顺从设定了过高期望而受到批评。因此，我对互惠孝道概念的出现很感兴趣。在互惠孝道中，子女对父母养育怀有真诚感激，任何义务感都发自内心——他们想回报恩情，也照顾父母。作为半个华人，我觉得有趣的是，在西方家庭生活中，孝道常被颠倒。大量讨论聚焦父母亏欠子女什么，而很少谈反向。例如，我注意到你没提到家人未来打算如何照顾你，或他们可能感到亏欠你什么。如果你确实采取凯恩斯式家庭方法，决定以可能惠及所有人的方式花钱，那么值得进行一些带儒家色彩的对话，不仅关于你亏欠别人什么，还关于你们彼此欣赏什么。你们可以共同反思，家庭因你们选择互相照顾的各种方式而更强大，而不仅仅因银行里有多少钱。我认为手边放一本《论语》很值得，其中充满智慧珠玑。我最近读到的一粒珍宝是……

刚刚读到的内容是关于如何最好地与他人相处：“君子和而不同，小人同而不和。”启示是，盲目跟随和复制他人的行为并不能让我们获益太多。在社会乃至家庭中，最和谐的方式是拥有互补的、相互契合的角色，就像合唱团中不同的音调一样。读到《纽约客》中亚历山德拉·施瓦茨关于死亡陪护师的文章时，我对变老这件事思考了很多。它提醒我们，除了直系亲属，其他人也能帮助度过生命中最艰难的时刻。至于有趣的内容：我喜欢娜塔莉·沃尔乔弗在《Quanta》上关于她（或任何人）为何是左撇子的调查。她探讨了左撇子的污名化和神经科学，以及一个理论：人类习惯用右手，是因为它们曾经更利于赢得打斗。查看更多：建议 未来 完美 生活 金钱 你的看法可能不同 如何重建你破碎的注意力 Ozempic不再只是减肥故事 用最新的Vox填字游戏休息一下 你应该把钱花在退休上还是给孩子？哈桑·皮克没有退缩 播客 邮箱（必填）注册 提交邮箱即表示你同意我们的条款和隐私声明。本网站受reCAPTCHA保护，并适用谷歌隐私政策和服务条款。广告商内容 这是原生广告的标题

readings.title: 6 ways to give that aren’t about money
body: Good news: You can be a generous person without writing a bunch of checks. In fact, many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need. This type of giving is open to everyone.
Many of the most awe-inspiring and effective examples of generosity are gifts of time and energy, talent and love, custom-fitted to a specific need.

Not sure where to begin? Here are six gifts of time and attention that have the strong potential to spark ripple effects that affect millions, from head of TED Chris Anderson’s new book, Infectious Generosity .

Zen master Thich Nhat Hanh taught that attention is the most precious gift we can give someone. This is where generosity starts — with a willingness to stop focusing on ourselves and to instead pay attention to someone else and their needs. From that act of connection, anything can happen.

Truth is, it can be difficult. We spend much of our time lost in our own worlds. We are often reluctant to focus on the issues that others are dealing with. So we put up shields. And that means that many of the people who could really use our attention never feel seen by us. The generosity of attention is therefore the generosity of being willing to be a little uncomfortable, to take down those shields, to give up some time, to risk coming to care about someone else.
Whether you stop and have a meaningful connection with a person in need or spend 30 minutes researching a cause you think might matter, you have already begun your generosity journey.

In our connected era, there’s a type of generosity that matters more than ever: a willingness to reach out to those with whom we disagree with. Many disputes today play out in public online. Huge audiences can become glued to online feuds. What if we could bring a satisfying resolution to more of these conflicts?

It’s hard to reach out to our critics. This is a particularly challenging form of the generosity mindset. You are sacrificing your personal comfort for the greater good of bringing people together. But if you’re successful, there’s a powerful knock-on benefit: You are helping change the tone of public discussion today. That’s a gift to all of us.
The single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.
In countless circumstances, the single greatest gift we can give is knowledge — knowledge that solves a problem, fills a need or opens a pathway forward.

Our single biggest piece of advice to someone coming to speak on the TED stage is to think of their talk not as an opportunity to pitch something (like a business or a cause) but rather as a gift. It is a chance to freely share valuable ideas with the audience. And those ideas have the potential to impact a listener’s life for years to come.

If you possess knowledge that others may benefit from, consider how you could share it to create ripple effects. What may take you a few hours to prepare and act on could light up someone’s life — and that could just be the beginning.

In our connected age, the networks we have access to matter more than ever. Therefore, one of the most important forms of viral generosity is to help people connect with others. The simplest way to do this is to make an introduction.

As psychologist and TED speaker Adam Grant has argued, an introduction can be fairly easy to give — and unbelievably valuable to receive. Ask many people how they met their partner, got their dream job or found the perfect collaborator for their creative project, and the answer will often be the same: someone — a friend, a neighbor, a colleague — introduced them to the right person. What you’re effectively doing is giving someone else access to your network of resources. And those introductions can have exponential consequences.

In his remarkable book Human Universals , anthropologist Donald Brown documented how hospitality is one of hundreds of human behaviors that have been observed in every single culture ever studied. But if hospitality is so ubiquitous (and so pleasant), is it really a form of generosity? Well, yes. Quite apart from any costs involved, it takes effort to invite someone over, whether friends or possible future friends. It’s easier just to watch the next episode of the TV series you’re into.
So how can hospitality contribute to infectious generosity? Hospitality taps into our deepest instincts for connection to one another. And each experience of it evokes a desire to reciprocate.
People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment.

Pioneering artist Lily Yeh was approached by the dancer and choreographer Arthur L. Hall to undertake a community art project in a derelict, abandoned plot in her home city of Philadelphia. “I was interested but totally scared,” Yeh recalled. “I had little resources and no experience in working outdoors in a community setting. I wanted to run away, but I did not want to see a coward in the mirror. So I stepped into the project.”

The community project became the Village of Arts and Humanities, an art park full of trees, sculptures and mosaics created by local adults and children in collaboration with Yeh. Yeh’s work led her to a profound realization: that creating beauty in public spaces is profoundly healing and transformative for communities.

People need money, food, shelter and healthcare, to be sure. But we also yearn for beauty, wonder, laughter, transcendence — all elements of enchantment. Those who can enchant can offer a gift of immense value.

##段落

6种不花钱的给予方式

好消息：你不必写下一堆支票，也能成为一个慷慨的人。事实上，许多最令人敬畏且最有效的慷慨之举，是量身定制地满足特定需求的时间、精力、才华与爱的馈赠。这种给予方式对每个人开放。

许多最令人敬畏且最有效的慷慨之举，是量身定制地满足特定需求的时间、精力、才华与爱的馈赠。

不知道从何开始？以下是六种时间与关注力的馈赠，它们有巨大潜力激发涟漪效应，影响数百万人——摘自TED负责人克里斯·安德森的新书《传染性慷慨》。

##段落

1. 转移注意力
禅宗大师一行禅师教导说，关注是我们能给予他人最珍贵的礼物。这就是慷慨的起点——愿意停止关注自己，转而关注他人及其需求。从这种联结的行为出发，任何事情都可能发生。

事实是，这并不容易。我们大部分时间都迷失在自己的世界里。我们常常不愿去关注他人正在处理的问题。于是我们竖起盾牌。这意味着许多真正需要我们的关注的人，从未感受到被我们看见。因此，关注的慷慨，就是愿意让自己稍微不舒服、卸下那些盾牌、放弃一些时间、冒险去在乎他人的慷慨。

无论你是停下来与需要帮助的人建立一次有意义的联结，还是花30分钟研究一个你认为可能重要的议题，你都已经开始了你的慷慨之旅。

##段落

2. 搭建桥梁
在我们这个互联的时代，有一种慷慨比以往任何时候都更重要：愿意主动接触与我们意见相左的人。如今许多争端都在线上公开上演。大量观众可能会紧盯网络纷争。如果我们能为更多这样的冲突带来令人满意的解决方案呢？

主动接触批评者很难。这是慷慨心态中特别具有挑战性的一种形式。你是在牺牲个人的舒适，为了将人们聚在一起的更大善益。但如果你成功了，会有一个强大的附带好处：你在帮助改变当今公共讨论的基调。这是给我们所有人的一份礼物。

我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

##段落

3. 分享知识
在无数情境中，我们能给予的最大礼物是知识——能解决问题、满足需求或开辟前进道路的知识。

我们对某人的最大建议是——

登上TED舞台演讲，关键在于将自己的演讲视为一份礼物，而非推销（如推广某项业务或事业）的机会。这是一个向听众自由分享宝贵想法的契机，而这些想法有可能在多年后持续影响听众的生活。
如果你拥有能让他人受益的知识，请思考如何分享它以产生涟漪效应。你可能只需花几个小时准备并付诸行动，却可能点亮某人的一生——而这或许只是开始。
4. 促成连接
在这个互联时代，我们所能触及的人脉网络比以往任何时候都更为重要。因此，病毒式慷慨最重要的形式之一就是帮助人们与他人建立联系。最简单的方式就是进行引荐。
正如心理学家兼TED演讲者亚当·格兰特所主张的那样，引荐之举对给予者而言相当容易，而对接受者来说却价值非凡。问问许多人他们是如何遇到伴侣、获得梦想工作或为创意项目找到完美合作者的，答案往往如出一辙：有人——朋友、邻居或同事——将他们引荐给了合适的人。你实际上是在为他人打开通向自己资源网络的大门，而这些引荐可能带来指数级的连锁效应。
5. 展现好客
人类学家唐纳德·布朗在其杰出著作《人类共性》中记录道，好客是已在每个被研究文化中观察到的数百种人类行为之一。但如果好客如此普遍（且如此令人愉悦），它真的是慷慨的一种形式吗？是的，确实如此。撇开涉及的任何成本不谈，邀请他人来访——无论是朋友还是潜在的新朋友——都需要付出努力。仅仅观看你正在追的下一集电视剧要容易得多。
那么好客如何促进传染性慷慨呢？好客触及了我们与他人建立联系的最深层本能，而每一次这样的体验都会激发回报的渴望。
人们当然需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健，但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑和超越——这些都是迷醉人心的元素。
6. 创造迷醉
先锋艺术家莉莉·叶曾被舞蹈家兼编舞家亚瑟·L·霍尔邀请，在她家乡费城一块废弃荒芜的地块上开展社区艺术项目。“我感兴趣但又完全害怕，”叶回忆道，“我资源匮乏，也没有在社区环境中进行户外工作的经验。我想逃跑，但我不想在镜子里看到懦夫。所以我踏入了这个项目。”
这个社区项目后来成为“艺术与人文之村”，一个充满树木、雕塑和马赛克艺术品的艺术公园，由当地成年人创作——

##段落
叶与青少年及儿童的合作让她深刻意识到：在公共空间创造美，对社区具有深远的疗愈与变革力量。

##段落
人们确实需要金钱、食物、住所和医疗保健。但我们也渴望美、惊奇、欢笑与超越——这些都是“魅力”的要素。能够赋予魅力的人，便能赠予一份无比珍贵的礼物。

readings.title: The Iran war’s mental toll on US sailors
body: Politics / Donald Trump / The Logoff The Iran war’s mental toll on US sailors ﻿Sailors are sounding the alarm about conditions on the USS Lincoln. by Cameron Peters Aug 13, 2026, 9:55 PM UTC Gift The USS Abraham Lincoln deployed in the Arabian Sea on April 16, 2026. US Navy via Getty Images Cameron Peters is a staff editor at Vox. This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here . Welcome to The Logoff: The cracks are starting to show in President Donald Trump’s Iran campaign. What’s happening? Conditions on a US warship deployed in the Middle East have grown so dire, multiple sailors have reportedly tried to go overboard (at least one did so but was rescued safely, according to CNN ). The attempts to jump overboard comes as family members of sailors are raising concerns with Democratic lawmakers about deteriorating mental health on the ship amid sanitation issues and shortages of food and basic supplies . The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has been deployed for more than 250 days, starting last November, including a stretch of more than 200 days at sea — a modern record. Its deployment was supposed to end months ago, in May, but has continued as Trump’s Iran war stretches on . How is the administration responding? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that reports about conditions on the Lincoln are “completely misrepresented.” Help is on the way for the Lincoln, though, with another US aircraft carrier en route to the area to replace it ( according to the Wall Street Journal , the replacement was already planned, and not in response to deteriorating conditions on the Lincoln). Five months of war with Iran Why does this matter? Conditions on the Lincoln are not the only recent stumbling block for the US war with Iran. Earlier this month, we learned more about the US’s increasingly serious shortages of key offensive and defensive missiles, including THAAD and Patriot interceptors used to protect US troops and allies. On top of that, the Washington Post reported Thursday that the US has run through around a quarter of its Reaper drones, which cost tens of millions of dollars apiece. It’s the latest example of how the math of the war is starting to slant against the US: Reaper drones and Patriot missiles are incredibly expensive, while Iran has figured out how to mass-produce attack drones on the cheap. And with no end in sight, shortages and situations like the Lincoln will only become a larger problem. Email (required) Sign Up By submitting your email, you agree to our Terms and Privacy Notice . This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply. Here’s some good news from my colleague Adam Clark Estes: As wrecked as your attention span may feel, it’s not permanently degraded. He talked with attention experts to figure out how to repair his, and how we can all do the same. You can read his full story here with a gift link — and then, for all of our brains’ sake, let’s log off. We’ll see you back here tomorrow.
